lesson.title: Getting an Intuitive Feel for Limits Before Proving Anything
lesson.summary: Building a table of function values on either side of a target point turns the abstract idea of a limit into something you can watch happen, and that intuition is what later algebraic techniques are trying to formalize.
lesson.body:
Before tackling algebraic techniques or formal proofs, it pays to build intuition for limits the most direct way possible: by watching numbers. Choose input values that creep closer and closer to the target, plug each one into the function, and watch what the outputs do. This numerical, hands-on approach will not prove a limit exists in the rigorous sense, but it builds the mental picture that all the later algebra is trying to formalize, and it catches mistakes that pure symbol manipulation can miss.

Take f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) and investigate lim(x to 2) f(x) using a table, approaching from below and above. From the left: x = 1.9 gives f(1.9) = (3.61 - 4)/(1.9 - 2) = (-0.39)/(-0.1) = 3.9. x = 1.99 gives f(1.99) = (3.9601 - 4)/(1.99 - 2) = (-0.0399)/(-0.01) = 3.99. x = 1.999 gives 3.999. From the right: x = 2.1 gives f(2.1) = (4.41 - 4)/(2.1 - 2) = 0.41/0.1 = 4.1. x = 2.01 gives f(2.01) = (4.0401 - 4)/(2.01 - 2) = 0.0401/0.01 = 4.01. x = 2.001 gives 4.001.

Both columns are squeezing toward the same number, 4, from opposite sides, even though x = 2 itself makes the formula 0/0 and is excluded from the domain. That squeeze, both directions closing in on one common value, is exactly what "the limit is 4" means intuitively, and it matches the algebraic shortcut: (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) = (x - 2)(x + 2)/(x - 2) = x + 2 for x not equal to 2, and x + 2 approaches 4 as x approaches 2.

Not every table settles down like this one does. Try the same approach on g(x) = 1/x^2 as x approaches 0: at x = 0.1, g(0.1) = 100; at x = 0.01, g(0.01) = 10,000; at x = 0.001, g(0.001) = 1,000,000. Instead of squeezing toward a fixed number, the outputs keep growing without bound the closer x gets to 0, from either side. A table like this is telling you something too, just not "the limit is some number L." It is showing a function that does not settle down at all, a case later sections will learn to describe precisely.

The intuitive, table-based approach has real shortcomings: a function can look like it is converging over a small range of test values and then misbehave further in, especially with oscillating functions, so tables are a sense-making tool, not a substitute for algebraic proof once one is available. Still, this is the right way to first meet a new limit. Build the table, watch the trend from both sides, form a guess about L, and only afterward reach for algebra or limit laws to confirm the guess rigorously. Skipping straight to formulas without ever watching numbers converge tends to produce students who can compute limits but cannot explain what a limit actually is, which defeats the purpose. A good rule of thumb: if you cannot sketch or describe what the table of values would look like for a brand-new limit, you are not yet ready to trust an algebraic shortcut applied to it.
